1	# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema
2	
3	Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
4	Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points
5	
6	Part of #35
7	
8	## Why
9	
10	`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
11	without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
12	Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
13	providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
14	shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
15	casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
16	that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
17	written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
18	confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.
19	
20	The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
21	to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
22	in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
23	of it.
24	
25	## What to do
26	
27	Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
28	`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
29	unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
30	schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
31	providers.
32	
33	Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
34	not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
35	resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.
36	
37	A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
38	so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
39	`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
40	generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
41	it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
42	there is no opt-out flag.
43	
44	Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.
45	
46	## Acceptance criteria
47	
48	- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
49	      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
50	      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
51	- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
52	      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
53	      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
54	      count is `0`
55	- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
56	      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
57	      exactly once
58	- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
59	      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
60	      **not** contain the offending value
61	- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
62	      that the thrown message names the tool
63	- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
64	      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
65	- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
66	- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
67	      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
68	      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
69	      round
70	- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
71	      pinned by a test
72	- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
73	      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
74	      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
75	      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
76	      containing that field's value
77	- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
78	      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
79	      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
80	      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
81	- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
82	      `devDependencies`, and
83	      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
84	- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
85	      merely present
86	- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
87	      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
88	      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
89	      returned to the model rather than thrown
90	- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
91	      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
92	      properties pass through unmodified
93	- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
94	      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
95	      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
96	      bump is MINOR
97	- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
98	      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
99	      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
100	      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
101	- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
102	      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
103	      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
104	- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
105	      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface
106	
107	## Tech notes
108	
109	Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
110	`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
111	WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
112	the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
113	`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.
114	
115	Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
116	class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
117	direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
118	throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
119	evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
120	valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
121	owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
122	authorization model); retry, timeout
123	and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
124	written against this contract later.
125	
126

# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.

The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
of it.

## What to do

Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
providers.

Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.

A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
there is no opt-out flag.

Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
      count is `0`
- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
      exactly once
- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
      **not** contain the offending value
- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
      that the thrown message names the tool
- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
      round
- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
      pinned by a test
- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
      containing that field's value
- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
      `devDependencies`, and
      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
      merely present
- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
      returned to the model rather than thrown
- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
      properties pass through unmodified
- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
      bump is MINOR
- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface

## Tech notes

Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.

Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
authorization model); retry, timeout
and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
written against this contract later.

1	# HAL Engine System Specification
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	HAL Engine is a generic, production-ready AI chat server framework designed to abstract away the complexity of building AI-powered chat backends. It provides a pluggable architecture for AI providers, tools, authentication, session management, and transport, allowing developers to focus on domain-specific logic rather than infrastructure plumbing.
6	
7	The system handles core patterns including streaming responses, tool execution loops, WebSocket connections, session persistence, and message orchestration. It is structured as a layered application with clear separation of concerns from core types through infrastructure and transport.
8	
9	**Primary Language**: TypeScript (ES2022, strict mode)  
10	**Entry Point**: `src/config.ts` (`createHalEngine()` factory function)
11	
12	---
13	
14	## Key Capabilities
15	
16	### 1. Multi-Provider Support
17	
18	- **AWS Bedrock** - `sendMessage` implemented, supporting Amazon Nova and other Bedrock models; `generateStructured` throws
19	- **Google Vertex AI** - both `AIProvider` methods implemented
20	- **OpenAI / ChatGPT** (stub with guidance for implementation)
21	- **Anthropic / Claude** (stub with guidance for implementation)
22	- **Mock Provider** (built-in for testing)
23	
24	Providers are abstractly defined via the `AIProvider` interface and instantiated through the `createProvider()` factory. A method that is not implemented throws a descriptive error carrying implementation guidance. Status is per method rather than per provider, and `README.md` carries the only matrix - a second copy would drift.
25	
26	### 2. Tool System
27	
28	- Dynamic tool registration via `ToolRegistry`
29	- JSON Schema tool definitions, declared per tool and forwarded to the model; the schema describes the input the model should produce and is NOT enforced before the executor runs
30	- Parallel tool execution within configurable tool loops
31	- Tool response normalization (supports both simple strings and structured content)
32	- Context-aware tool execution: the executor receives the caller's identity (`userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`) and the auth headers the session carries, forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade or the HTTP chat request, not the conversation history
33	- Configurable maximum tool loop iterations (default: 5)
34	
35	### 3. Real-Time Streaming
36	
37	- WebSocket-based bi-directional communication
38	- Entry-based protocol (supports User, Assistant, Thinking, Tool, and error entries)
39	- Thinking tag parsing for handling model reasoning artifacts
40	- Delta-based streaming for efficient bandwidth usage
41	- Automatic heartbeat mechanism (default: 30-second interval)
42	
43	### 4. Pluggable Authentication
44	
45	- Custom WebSocket authentication via `WsAuthenticator` function
46	- Express middleware-based HTTP authentication via `HttpAuthMiddleware`, which must attach a `user` to the `AuthenticatedRequest`
47	- Session binding to authenticated users
48	- User context propagated throughout request lifecycle
49	
50	### 5. Session Management
51	
52	- In-memory default session store (`InMemorySessionStore`)
53	- Pluggable interface for custom stores (Redis, database, etc.)
54	- Automatic session lifecycle (creation, retrieval, cleanup)
55	- Fire-and-forget `onConnect` and `onDisconnect` hooks, neither awaited and neither able to fail a connection
56	- Session persistence across WebSocket reconnections
57	
58	### 6. Configurable Prompts
59	
60	- Injectable system prompt builder (`PromptBuilder`)
61	- Identity, domain context, and response guideline configuration
62	- Dynamic prompt composition from templates
63	
64	### 7. HTTP + WebSocket Server
65	
66	- Express.js v5 application with full CORS support
67	- WebSocket server built on `ws` library
68	- Configurable base path (default: `/hal`)
69	- Type-safe route definitions
70	
71	---
72	
73	## Core Data Model
74	
75	### Message Flow
76	
77	**Incoming Messages** (`IncomingMessage` type):
78	
79	- `UserMessage`: User-provided text input with optional metadata
80	- `Ping`: WebSocket heartbeat
81	
82	**Outgoing Messages** (`OutgoingMessage` type):
83	
84	- `ConnectedMessage`: Initial handshake after WebSocket connection
85	- `EntryUpsertMessage`: New or updated conversation entry
86	- `EntryDeltaMessage`: Streaming content delta
87	- `EntryCommitMessage`: Entry finalization marker
88	- `EntrySkipMessage`: Skip tool/response generation
89	- `ErrorMessage`: Error with code and details
90	- `PongMessage`: Heartbeat acknowledgment
91	- `StreamEndMessage`: End of streaming sequence
92	
93	### Session Model
94	
95	**ChatSession**:
96	
97	- `id`: Unique session identifier (UUID)
98	- `userId`: Authenticated user identifier
99	- `entries`: Array of conversation entries
100	- `createdAt`: Session creation timestamp
101	- `updatedAt`: Last activity timestamp
102	
103	**Entry Types**:
104	
105	- `UserEntry`: Text message from user
106	- `AssistantEntry`: AI-generated response with tool calls
107	- `ThinkingEntry`: Internal reasoning (parsed from models that support thinking)
108	- `ToolEntry`: Tool execution metadata and results
109	- `SessionEntry`: Marker for session lifecycle events
110	
111	### AI Communication Model
112	
113	**Message** types:
114	
115	- `TextMessage`: Simple text content
116	- `ToolUseMessage`: Tool invocation with arguments
117	- `ToolResultMessage`: Tool execution result
118	- `ToolCallContent`: Structured tool call representation
119	- `ToolResultContent`: Structured tool result representation
120	
121	**ToolDefinition**:
122	<!-- doc-block: none -- a JSON message payload, not a TypeScript declaration -->
123	```typescript
124	{
125	  name: string;
126	  description: string;
127	  inputSchema: JSONSchema;
128	}
129	```
130	
131	**Tool Response Variants**:
132	
133	- String: Direct text response
134	- Object with `content`: Rich structured content
135	- Object with `entries`: Multiple message entries
136	- Normalized to internal format via `normalizeToolResponse()`
137	
138	---
139	
140	## User Roles
141	
142	### 1. **System Administrator**
143	
144	- Configures `HalEngineConfig` during initialization
145	- Selects AI provider and region
146	- Defines authentication strategy
147	- Sets rate limits and tool execution constraints
148	- Manages session store backend
149	- Configures CORS and network settings
150	
151	### 2. **Application Developer**
152	
153	- Implements custom `WsAuthenticator` and optional `HttpAuthMiddleware`
154	- Registers domain-specific tools via `ToolRegistry`
155	- Defines prompt templates and system instructions
156	- Implements custom `SessionStore` if needed
157	- Handles `onConnect`/`onDisconnect` lifecycle hooks, both returning `void | Promise<void>`
158	- Consumes published API from `createHalEngine()`
159	
160	### 3. **End User**
161	
162	- Connects via WebSocket with authentication token
163	- Sends `UserMessage` entries with text input
164	- Receives streaming `EntryUpsert`/`EntryDelta` messages
165	- Observes tool execution through entry protocol
166	- Maintains session across reconnections
167	
168	### 4. **AI Model (Provider)**
169	
170	- Processes chat history and system prompts
171	- Generates text responses and tool calls
172	- Streams content in chunks
173	- Returns usage metadata (tokens, cost estimation)
174	- Validates tool calls against schemas
175	
176	---
177	
178	## Business Rules
179	
180	### 1. Tool Execution
181	
182	- Tools execute only when explicitly requested by the AI model
183	- Maximum tool loop iterations enforce termination (prevents infinite loops)
184	- Tools execute in response to explicit `ToolCall` objects from the model
185	- Tool results are returned to the model for incorporation into response
186	- Tool failures are communicated via `ToolResultMessage` with error content
187	
188	### 2. Message Ordering
189	
190	- User messages must precede assistant responses
191	- Tool results must follow corresponding tool calls
192	- Thinking entries (when present) appear before tool calls or text
193	- All entries within a single assistant response are committed atomically
194	- Session history is immutable after commit
195	
196	### 3. Authentication & Authorization
197	
198	- WebSocket connections require successful `WsAuthenticator` callback
199	- Invalid tokens result in connection rejection
200	- Each session is bound to exactly one authenticated user
201	- User context is available to tools and infrastructure components
202	- The chat routes require an identified user: with no middleware configured, or middleware that attaches no usable `user.id`, they answer `401`
203	
204	### 4. Session Lifecycle
205	
206	- Sessions are created on first successful WebSocket connection
207	- Sessions persist across disconnections (reconnection support)
208	- `onDisconnect` hook fires when session is abandoned (configurable timeout)
209	- Session entries are append-only (immutable history)
210	- Session cleanup follows configurable eviction policy
211	
212	### 5. Streaming & Response Handling
213	
214	- Streaming begins immediately upon receiving user message
215	- Thinking content is parsed from XML tags (provider-dependent)
216	- Deltas are sent as soon as available (streaming chunks)
217	- Complete entries are committed before next entry begins
218	- Client must handle partial messages due to network conditions
219	
220	### 6. Tool Response Normalization
221	
222	- Tool executors return `string`, object with `content`, or object with `entries`
223	- Framework normalizes all variants to internal representation
224	- Tool results are validated against original tool definition schema
225	- Malformed responses result in error entries
226	
227	### 7. Provider Compatibility
228	
229	- Provider selection is immutable per engine instance
230	- Provider-specific configuration is validated at startup
231	- Missing provider dependencies (e.g., AWS SDK) result in clear error messages
232	- All providers implement identical `AIProvider` interface
233	
234	---
235	
236	## Success Metrics
237	
238	### Operational Metrics
239	
240	1. **Availability**: WebSocket server uptime and connection stability
241	2. **Latency**:
242	   - Time to first token (TTFT) from model
243	   - End-to-end response time (user message → final entry commit)
244	3. **Throughput**: Concurrent WebSocket connections supported
245	4. **Error Rate**: Failed messages, tool execution errors, provider failures
246	
247	### Integration Metrics
248	
249	1. **Tool Success Rate**: Percentage of tool calls that execute without error
250	2. **Tool Loop Efficiency**: Average iterations before response completion
251	3. **Streaming Efficiency**: Chunk size and delta frequency
252	
253	### Developer Experience Metrics
254	
255	1. **Time to Integration**: Hours to implement custom provider or tool
256	2. **Configuration Complexity**: Lines of code for basic setup
257	3. **Documentation Coverage**: Completeness of docs/ directory
258	
259	### Business Metrics
260	
261	1. **Provider Cost Per Interaction**: Token usage × provider pricing
262	2. **Session Persistence**: Reconnection success rate
263	3. **Authentication Success Rate**: Percentage of valid auth attempts
264	
265	### Reliability Metrics
266	
267	1. **Message Delivery Guarantee**: No lost messages within a session
268	2. **Tool Execution Idempotency**: Safe to retry failed tool calls
269	3. **Provider Fallback**: Time to detect provider failure and escalate
270	
271	---
272	
273	## Architecture Overview
274	
275	The system is organized into five layers plus a cross-cutting utilities layer:
276	
277	- **Layer 0 (Shared)**: Logger and common utilities
278	- **Layer 1 (Types)**: Core type definitions (AI, session, messages, auth, stores)
279	- **Layer 2 (Providers)**: AI provider implementations (Bedrock, Vertex, OpenAI, Anthropic, Mock)
280	- **Layer 3 (Infrastructure)**: Stores (session, prompt, usage), builders (prompt), parsers (thinking tags)
281	- **Layer 4 (Orchestration)**: Chat orchestrator, tool registry, conversation context, entry management
282	- **Layer 5 (Transport)**: Express app, WebSocket server, HTTP/WebSocket routes
283	
284	Each layer depends only on layers below it, ensuring clean separation of concerns.
285	
286	---
287	
288	## Configuration & Deployment
289	
290	### Required Configuration
291	
292	- `provider`: Type and credentials for selected AI provider
293	- `prompt`: System identity and context instructions
294	- `auth.ws`: WebSocket authentication function
295	
296	### Optional Configuration
297	
298	- `tools`: Custom tool registry (defaults to empty)
299	- `session`: Custom session store (defaults to in-memory)
300	- `transport`: Port, CORS, base path, heartbeat interval
301	- `auth.http`: Express middleware for HTTP endpoints
302	- `orchestrator`: Max tool rounds, context config, lifecycle hooks

# HAL Engine System Specification

## Overview

HAL Engine is a generic, production-ready AI chat server framework designed to abstract away the complexity of building AI-powered chat backends. It provides a pluggable architecture for AI providers, tools, authentication, session management, and transport, allowing developers to focus on domain-specific logic rather than infrastructure plumbing.

The system handles core patterns including streaming responses, tool execution loops, WebSocket connections, session persistence, and message orchestration. It is structured as a layered application with clear separation of concerns from core types through infrastructure and transport.

**Primary Language**: TypeScript (ES2022, strict mode)  
**Entry Point**: `src/config.ts` (`createHalEngine()` factory function)

---

## Key Capabilities

### 1. Multi-Provider Support

- **AWS Bedrock** - `sendMessage` implemented, supporting Amazon Nova and other Bedrock models; `generateStructured` throws
- **Google Vertex AI** - both `AIProvider` methods implemented
- **OpenAI / ChatGPT** (stub with guidance for implementation)
- **Anthropic / Claude** (stub with guidance for implementation)
- **Mock Provider** (built-in for testing)

Providers are abstractly defined via the `AIProvider` interface and instantiated through the `createProvider()` factory. A method that is not implemented throws a descriptive error carrying implementation guidance. Status is per method rather than per provider, and `README.md` carries the only matrix - a second copy would drift.

### 2. Tool System

- Dynamic tool registration via `ToolRegistry`
- JSON Schema tool definitions, declared per tool and forwarded to the model; the schema describes the input the model should produce and is NOT enforced before the executor runs
- Parallel tool execution within configurable tool loops
- Tool response normalization (supports both simple strings and structured content)
- Context-aware tool execution: the executor receives the caller's identity (`userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`) and the auth headers the session carries, forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade or the HTTP chat request, not the conversation history
- Configurable maximum tool loop iterations (default: 5)

### 3. Real-Time Streaming

- WebSocket-based bi-directional communication
- Entry-based protocol (supports User, Assistant, Thinking, Tool, and error entries)
- Thinking tag parsing for handling model reasoning artifacts
- Delta-based streaming for efficient bandwidth usage
- Automatic heartbeat mechanism (default: 30-second interval)

### 4. Pluggable Authentication

- Custom WebSocket authentication via `WsAuthenticator` function
- Express middleware-based HTTP authentication via `HttpAuthMiddleware`, which must attach a `user` to the `AuthenticatedRequest`
- Session binding to authenticated users
- User context propagated throughout request lifecycle

### 5. Session Management

- In-memory default session store (`InMemorySessionStore`)
- Pluggable interface for custom stores (Redis, database, etc.)
- Automatic session lifecycle (creation, retrieval, cleanup)
- Fire-and-forget `onConnect` and `onDisconnect` hooks, neither awaited and neither able to fail a connection
- Session persistence across WebSocket reconnections

### 6. Configurable Prompts

- Injectable system prompt builder (`PromptBuilder`)
- Identity, domain context, and response guideline configuration
- Dynamic prompt composition from templates

### 7. HTTP + WebSocket Server

- Express.js v5 application with full CORS support
- WebSocket server built on `ws` library
- Configurable base path (default: `/hal`)
- Type-safe route definitions

---

## Core Data Model

### Message Flow

**Incoming Messages** (`IncomingMessage` type):

- `UserMessage`: User-provided text input with optional metadata
- `Ping`: WebSocket heartbeat

**Outgoing Messages** (`OutgoingMessage` type):

- `ConnectedMessage`: Initial handshake after WebSocket connection
- `EntryUpsertMessage`: New or updated conversation entry
- `EntryDeltaMessage`: Streaming content delta
- `EntryCommitMessage`: Entry finalization marker
- `EntrySkipMessage`: Skip tool/response generation
- `ErrorMessage`: Error with code and details
- `PongMessage`: Heartbeat acknowledgment
- `StreamEndMessage`: End of streaming sequence

### Session Model

**ChatSession**:

- `id`: Unique session identifier (UUID)
- `userId`: Authenticated user identifier
- `entries`: Array of conversation entries
- `createdAt`: Session creation timestamp
- `updatedAt`: Last activity timestamp

**Entry Types**:

- `UserEntry`: Text message from user
- `AssistantEntry`: AI-generated response with tool calls
- `ThinkingEntry`: Internal reasoning (parsed from models that support thinking)
- `ToolEntry`: Tool execution metadata and results
- `SessionEntry`: Marker for session lifecycle events

### AI Communication Model

**Message** types:

- `TextMessage`: Simple text content
- `ToolUseMessage`: Tool invocation with arguments
- `ToolResultMessage`: Tool execution result
- `ToolCallContent`: Structured tool call representation
- `ToolResultContent`: Structured tool result representation

**ToolDefinition**:
<!-- doc-block: none -- a JSON message payload, not a TypeScript declaration -->
```typescript
{
  name: string;
  description: string;
  inputSchema: JSONSchema;
}
```

**Tool Response Variants**:

- String: Direct text response
- Object with `content`: Rich structured content
- Object with `entries`: Multiple message entries
- Normalized to internal format via `normalizeToolResponse()`

---

## User Roles

### 1. **System Administrator**

- Configures `HalEngineConfig` during initialization
- Selects AI provider and region
- Defines authentication strategy
- Sets rate limits and tool execution constraints
- Manages session store backend
- Configures CORS and network settings

### 2. **Application Developer**

- Implements custom `WsAuthenticator` and optional `HttpAuthMiddleware`
- Registers domain-specific tools via `ToolRegistry`
- Defines prompt templates and system instructions
- Implements custom `SessionStore` if needed
- Handles `onConnect`/`onDisconnect` lifecycle hooks, both returning `void | Promise<void>`
- Consumes published API from `createHalEngine()`

### 3. **End User**

- Connects via WebSocket with authentication token
- Sends `UserMessage` entries with text input
- Receives streaming `EntryUpsert`/`EntryDelta` messages
- Observes tool execution through entry protocol
- Maintains session across reconnections

### 4. **AI Model (Provider)**

- Processes chat history and system prompts
- Generates text responses and tool calls
- Streams content in chunks
- Returns usage metadata (tokens, cost estimation)
- Validates tool calls against schemas

---

## Business Rules

### 1. Tool Execution

- Tools execute only when explicitly requested by the AI model
- Maximum tool loop iterations enforce termination (prevents infinite loops)
- Tools execute in response to explicit `ToolCall` objects from the model
- Tool results are returned to the model for incorporation into response
- Tool failures are communicated via `ToolResultMessage` with error content

### 2. Message Ordering

- User messages must precede assistant responses
- Tool results must follow corresponding tool calls
- Thinking entries (when present) appear before tool calls or text
- All entries within a single assistant response are committed atomically
- Session history is immutable after commit

### 3. Authentication & Authorization

- WebSocket connections require successful `WsAuthenticator` callback
- Invalid tokens result in connection rejection
- Each session is bound to exactly one authenticated user
- User context is available to tools and infrastructure components
- The chat routes require an identified user: with no middleware configured, or middleware that attaches no usable `user.id`, they answer `401`

### 4. Session Lifecycle

- Sessions are created on first successful WebSocket connection
- Sessions persist across disconnections (reconnection support)
- `onDisconnect` hook fires when session is abandoned (configurable timeout)
- Session entries are append-only (immutable history)
- Session cleanup follows configurable eviction policy

### 5. Streaming & Response Handling

- Streaming begins immediately upon receiving user message
- Thinking content is parsed from XML tags (provider-dependent)
- Deltas are sent as soon as available (streaming chunks)
- Complete entries are committed before next entry begins
- Client must handle partial messages due to network conditions

### 6. Tool Response Normalization

- Tool executors return `string`, object with `content`, or object with `entries`
- Framework normalizes all variants to internal representation
- Tool results are validated against original tool definition schema
- Malformed responses result in error entries

### 7. Provider Compatibility

- Provider selection is immutable per engine instance
- Provider-specific configuration is validated at startup
- Missing provider dependencies (e.g., AWS SDK) result in clear error messages
- All providers implement identical `AIProvider` interface

---

## Success Metrics

### Operational Metrics

1. **Availability**: WebSocket server uptime and connection stability
2. **Latency**:
   - Time to first token (TTFT) from model
   - End-to-end response time (user message → final entry commit)
3. **Throughput**: Concurrent WebSocket connections supported
4. **Error Rate**: Failed messages, tool execution errors, provider failures

### Integration Metrics

1. **Tool Success Rate**: Percentage of tool calls that execute without error
2. **Tool Loop Efficiency**: Average iterations before response completion
3. **Streaming Efficiency**: Chunk size and delta frequency

### Developer Experience Metrics

1. **Time to Integration**: Hours to implement custom provider or tool
2. **Configuration Complexity**: Lines of code for basic setup
3. **Documentation Coverage**: Completeness of docs/ directory

### Business Metrics

1. **Provider Cost Per Interaction**: Token usage × provider pricing
2. **Session Persistence**: Reconnection success rate
3. **Authentication Success Rate**: Percentage of valid auth attempts

### Reliability Metrics

1. **Message Delivery Guarantee**: No lost messages within a session
2. **Tool Execution Idempotency**: Safe to retry failed tool calls
3. **Provider Fallback**: Time to detect provider failure and escalate

---

## Architecture Overview

The system is organized into five layers plus a cross-cutting utilities layer:

- **Layer 0 (Shared)**: Logger and common utilities
- **Layer 1 (Types)**: Core type definitions (AI, session, messages, auth, stores)
- **Layer 2 (Providers)**: AI provider implementations (Bedrock, Vertex, OpenAI, Anthropic, Mock)
- **Layer 3 (Infrastructure)**: Stores (session, prompt, usage), builders (prompt), parsers (thinking tags)
- **Layer 4 (Orchestration)**: Chat orchestrator, tool registry, conversation context, entry management
- **Layer 5 (Transport)**: Express app, WebSocket server, HTTP/WebSocket routes

Each layer depends only on layers below it, ensuring clean separation of concerns.

---

## Configuration & Deployment

### Required Configuration

- `provider`: Type and credentials for selected AI provider
- `prompt`: System identity and context instructions
- `auth.ws`: WebSocket authentication function

### Optional Configuration

- `tools`: Custom tool registry (defaults to empty)
- `session`: Custom session store (defaults to in-memory)
- `transport`: Port, CORS, base path, heartbeat interval
- `auth.http`: Express middleware for HTTP endpoints
- `orchestrator`: Max tool rounds, context config, lifecycle hooks
- `onConnect`/`onDisconnect`: Lifecycle hooks, fire-and-forget
- `logger`: Custom logger instance

### Deployment Artifacts

- Builds to `dist/` directory (ES2022, ESM only - `type: module`, resolved through the `exports` map)
- Type definitions included (`dist/index.d.ts`)
- Published as npm package `@re-cinq/hal-engine`, Apache-2.0, `engines: node >=22`
- `@types/express`, `@types/node` and `@types/ws` are runtime `dependencies`, not dev: the emitted `.d.ts` files import `express`, `http`, `stream` and `ws`, so a consumer cannot type-check without them

---

## Development & Testing

- **TypeScript**: Strict mode, ES2022 target
- **Testing Framework**: Jest with ts-jest
- **Linting**: ESLint with flat config
- **Formatting**: Prettier
- **Development**: `tsx watch`, hot-reloading `example/server.ts`
- **Build**: TypeScript compiler, declarations only - the published build emits no source or declaration maps

# Tool Input Validation

| Field  | Value                |
| ------ | -------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |
| Status | Draft                |

`ToolRegistry.execute` currently calls the executor without checking the input it received against the tool's declared `inputSchema`. Every tool declares a JSON Schema that is forwarded verbatim to the AI providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The registry pushes this check onto each executor — differently each time, or not at all. This spec defines the validation contract so a malformed call fails predictably at the registry layer, once, and in a form the model can read and correct.

## Validation on execute

- When `execute` is called with input that fails the tool's declared `inputSchema` (for example, a missing required field), it returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the failing constraint — it does not call the executor, so a tool that relies on seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it ([validated by: rejects a call missing a required field and never invokes the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L7)).

- Because `execute` returns a `ToolResponse` on schema failure rather than throwing, the rejection text is forwarded to the model as a tool result in the next round's messages, giving the model the information it needs to issue a corrected call; the conversation does not end with a transport error ([validated by: a schema-invalid tool call does not throw so the model receives the rejection text and can retry](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L30)).

## Out of scope

Extra properties in valid input pass through to the executor unchanged — no coercion, no defaults, no stripping of additional properties. The `Unknown tool: <name>` throw for an unregistered name is unchanged. Output validation, hallucination detection, per-tool authorisation, and retry/timeout policy are out of scope.
